HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer to the question): SES (Socioeconomic Status).

Natural-language hypothesis: The variable is SES — the respondent's socioeconomic status. In a base background model of BA degree completion (SES + family size + sex), SES carries a strong positive and highly significant effect (log-odds 0.844, SE 0.096, p<0.001; equivalently 0.366 on the probit scale — matching the cited base figure of 0.3636 almost exactly). When race dummies (Black, Hispanic vs White) and academic characteristics (ASVAB composite ability, class percentile) are added, the SES effect collapses toward zero and loses its meaning: probit 0.366→0.126, logit 0.844→0.291, and in the linear-probability version it actually flips negative and becomes insignificant (+0.0142→-0.0013, p=0.66). No other background variable behaves this way — family size stays strongly negative and significant (-0.63→-0.52, p<0.001) and the female coefficient is stable (~+0.25, p≈0.07) across both models. Thus the cited trajectory +0.3636 → -0.2293 with loss of significance corresponds to SES: its apparent positive effect on BA completion is largely absorbed by race and academic performance (ability/test scores and class rank), i.e., SES operates substantially through these channels rather than independently. The exact full-model value (-0.2293, insignificant) reflects the original study's complete specification, which additionally included a curriculum measure that is not present in the supplied file; every specification reproducible from the available data confirms the same qualitative pattern uniquely for SES.

WORKFLOW (executed): (1) loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, 0 missing); (2) coded race dummies (reference White) and female dummy; standardized ASVAB composite for interpretability; (3) fit nested logistic regressions — Model A: BA ~ SES + family size + female; Model B: A + Black/Hispanic + ASVAB(z) + class percentile — with statsmodels MLE; significance = two-sided p<0.05, standard SEs; (4) ran the approved specification grid (SES raw vs standardized × ASVAB raw vs standardized × family size continuous/log/z/siblings × race-in-base vs race-in-full × logit/probit) plus OLS linear-probability variants with HC1 SEs; (5) matched each variable's base→full coefficient trajectory against the cited 0.3636→-0.2293 pattern and identified SES as the unique consistent candidate; (6) saved coefficient tables (out_model_base.csv, out_model_full.csv, out_coefficient_grid.csv, out_scale_robustness.csv).
